label: Thin glue

components: Fetch.ai watchdog agent on Agentverse (API), payment-event ingestion from x402/MoonPay testnet (API/glue), streaming payment graph with cycle and refund ping-pong detection (original, textbook), circuit-breaker rule (glue), Elastic dashboard (API), Claude explanation of flagged loops (prompt)

label: Not needed

label: API mashup
take: Bidding ROSCAs and chit-fund apps already exist; putting an LLM agent on each member's bid adds cost, not intelligence.
reasoning: An auction ROSCA is a well-understood mechanism: the highest discount wins the pot and the discount is shared, and chit-fund software and MoneyFellows already run it online. A member's bid is a function of cash need and rate, which a script computes better than a chat model. The genuinely hard problem, default risk after a member takes the pot, is handed to a CRS API call.
red_flag: The only depth is an API call for KYC, and pooled-savings products are regulated in most markets where they are popular.
components: Auction ROSCA round logic (original, small), one bidding agent per member (prompt), CRS KYC and income verification (API), collateral sizing rule (glue), Visa payouts (API), Convex state (API)

label: Nice to have
take: Real community, wrong fix: the auction monetizes members' desperation instead of reducing defaults or building credit.
reasoning: ROSCAs are used by hundreds of millions of people and the pains are real: default risk and credit invisibility. Agent bidding addresses neither, and introduces a predatory dynamic. The proven impact lever is credit-bureau reporting of on-time contributions, which my pivot B-P4 keeps.
red_flag: Agents bidding on behalf of low-income savers is a solution nobody in the circle asked for.
problem: A family saving through a tanda or susu risks a member skipping payments after taking the pot early, and their years of on-time payments build no credit history.
status_quo: Informal circles run on trust and group chats; nonprofits such as Mission Asset Fund formalize them and report payments to credit bureaus (68,000+ participants, average +168 credit-score points).
solution: Members' agents bid each round to take the pot early; CRS income verification and KYC decide who joins and how much collateral they post.
optimizes: Default losses inside circles and the price of early liquidity; the auction adds price discovery, not safety.
who: Savings-group users worldwide (Findex 2011: 19% of adults in Sub-Saharan Africa used a community savings group); millions in US immigrant communities (no reliable US count found).
harm: The auction makes the most cash-desperate member pay the steepest discount for the pot, turning mutual aid into a lender profiting from distress; collateral and income checks exclude the very people circles serve.

label: New angle

prior_art: MoneyFellows (Egypt, digital money circles, $60M+ raised, 8.5M users); ElGameya (Egypt, digital ROSCA, 7-figure round 2025); BX Smart Labs (Mexico, on-chain tandas, UNICEF fund)

buyer: Savings-circle members (diaspora and underbanked communities) through a platform fee
model: Take rate on the pot or a membership fee, plus a lending spread
wedge: US diaspora tanda and susu groups already running circles on WhatsApp

label: API mashup
take: This already exists as products: AgentScore and DJD Agent Score sell x402 reputation lookups over MCP, and Vouched raised $17M for Know Your Agent.
reasoning: Stripped down, it is KYC from CRS plus a scoring formula over payment rows, and none of it needs an LLM. A score built on 36 hours of synthetic transactions carries no signal, and the hard part of agent reputation, sybil agents washing their own history, is not addressed. Funded teams already ship the same lookup as an MCP tool.

label: Emerging

problem: A merchant or service asked to deliver before payment to an unknown AI agent cannot tell whether anyone accountable stands behind it.
status_quo: Prepayment (x402 is pay-before-serve), card-network agent tokens and signatures (Visa Intelligent Commerce, Trusted Agent Protocol), and funded startups: AgentScore scores agents from x402 history and Vouched sells Know Your Agent.

optimizes: Counterparty default losses on agent-to-agent credit; today almost no agent credit is extended, so the loss pool is small.
who: Agent platforms and API sellers; low thousands of businesses so far.
harm: Linking agents to their owners' consumer credit files spreads sensitive data and lets one bad score shut a person out of agent commerce.

label: Already exists

label: Thin glue
take: The right problem, but runtime MCP proxies with guardrails already exist, so the version that detects injections with a classifier is a wrapper.
reasoning: If quarantine fires because a classifier flagged the page, this is a detector with a graph drawing, and it fails the moment a judge writes an injection the classifier misses. Invariant's mcp-scan proxy and Enkrypt's MCP gateway already do runtime guardrails on tool traffic. The defensible version is deterministic: tag every value by provenance and block untrusted data from reaching sensitive tool arguments, as CaMeL does; that is a real system, so I merged it into my Fire Drill pivot.

components: Agent with MCP tools (API), injection detection on fetched pages (prompt classifier), tool-trust graph with quarantine (original if taint-based, glue if a toggle), live graph visualization (UI), Elastic logging (API)
hard_core: Taint propagation across tool calls could be one, but as written detection is a classifier and quarantine is a switch.

label: Emerging
take: Documented, growing problem and the right target (containment), but the note never says how compromise is detected.
reasoning: Toxic agent flows are documented (Invariant on GitHub MCP, General Analysis on Supabase MCP), and both OpenAI and the UK NCSC say to plan for injection succeeding. Containment is where damage gets cut. Detection by another LLM is noisy, so the quarantine has no reliable trigger; my pivot B-P1 adds Flytrap-style decoys as that trigger.
red_flag: Quarantine is only as good as its trigger, and the trigger is unspecified.

status_quo: Injection filters and guardrail products, least-privilege tokens, confirmation prompts users click through; OpenAI says prompt injection is unlikely ever to be fully solved, so limiting damage matters.
solution: Watch the agent's tool graph and quarantine compromised tools zero-trust style while the agent runs.
optimizes: Records exfiltrated and unauthorized actions per injection incident.
who: Every team running agents with MCP tools on private data; tens of thousands of companies and growing.
harm: Over-eager quarantine breaks legitimate workflows; a staged demo can overclaim detection rates.

label: Better execution

prior_art: Runlayer ($11M seed, MCP and agent security); Helmet Security ($9M, MCP monitoring); MCP-Shield, mcpwall and MCP Output Firewall (open source); Lakera (acquired by Check Point, reported ~$300M)

buyer: CISOs and platform security teams

wow: A judge hides an instruction in a web page; as the agent reads it, the tool graph turns red and the compromised tools are cut off.

status_quo: Gossip, and general play-money prediction markets that already cover anything.

label: Thin glue

Deterministic replay comes free from SpacetimeDB's reducer log rather than being engineered. Digits, Puzzle and YC's End Close already sell AI reconciliation, and monsters lower credibility with exactly the finance judges this targets.
red_flag: LLM-proposed matches with no correctness guarantee in front of finance judges.

label: Urgent
take: A big monthly pain, addressed by a game layer accountants would not pay for.

red_flag: Strip the game and it is a crowded reconciliation tool; keep it and finance buyers will not take it seriously.

status_quo: Excel plus close software (BlackLine, FloQast, Numeric) and newer AI agents such as Hyphenate's; per Ledge's 2025 benchmark, about half of teams still need more than five business days and Excel remains near-universal.
solution: Unmatched transactions spawn as monsters in a shared world; Claude proposes matches, accountants approve; deterministic replay is the audit trail.

who: Accountants and controllers at millions of companies.
harm: Gamified pressure to beat the boss nudges accountants to rubber-stamp AI matches, the opposite of what auditors want.

prior_art: Hyphenate (sponsor; close and bank-rec agents with human escalation); Maxima (Kleiner Perkins-backed close agents); End Close (YC); Puzzle (agent executes, human approves)

buyer: Controllers and accounting teams

label: Wrapper
take: Authorize now, capture later, with a voice prompt on top; payments infrastructure already ships the undo window.
reasoning: Stripe's manual capture reserves funds and lets you capture or release them later, which is the whole 'rollback before it settles' mechanic. Cartesia announces the purchase and STT listens for one word. Nothing here needs an LLM or original engineering, so it clones in an afternoon.
red_flag: Clone time is hours, and there is nothing for the Anthropic judge to score.
components: Intercept of agent purchases (glue), authorize-now-capture-later payment (API), Cartesia voice announcement and STT listening for 'cancel' (API), countdown timer (glue)
hard_core: none. A grace window is authorize-and-capture-later, which card payments already support.

label: Emerging
take: A sensible safety feature for agent checkout, but one that card networks and agent platforms are already building in.
reasoning: Consumer surveys show trust in agent purchases depends on approvals and recourse, so the need is real and emerging. A grace window is a feature of the payment flow, not a standalone product, and the people who feel the pain only occasionally hit it.
red_flag: Feature, not product: the networks own the settlement window.
problem: A person whose shopping agent is about to buy the wrong thing has no easy undo once it pays (OpenAI's Operator bought $31.43 of eggs without the confirmation it was supposed to ask for).
status_quo: Agent platforms ask for confirmation before paying, sometimes skip it; afterwards, returns and chargebacks, which merchants absorb because liability rules lag.
solution: Every agent purchase sits in a short grace window and is announced by voice; one word cancels before settlement.
optimizes: Unwanted agent purchases and resulting disputes; consumers' willingness to delegate (Accenture: only 9% open to fully autonomous purchases including payment).
who: Early shopping-agent users; small today, forecast to grow fast.
harm: Spoken purchase announcements leak private information in shared spaces; holds can be abused to tie up inventory.

label: New angle
take: A good feature that issuers and agent apps will build themselves; a thin company.
reasoning: Consumers say they want to cancel agent purchases (Nuvei reports 84%), but the fix is a pre-settlement hold plus a confirmation, which issuers and approval tools like Mercury, Reap and HumanLayer already approximate. The voice 'cancel?' moment is cute but short. Hard to defend once Visa or an issuer ships it.
red_flag: A feature, not a company; incumbents own the settlement window.
prior_art: Mercury Agent Cards (human-set limits, Aug 2026); Reap passkey-approved spending mandates; HumanLayer (YC, approval gates for agent actions); Nuvei consumer research on reversing agent purchases
why_now: Agents now buy with cards (Visa Intelligent Commerce, agent cards) and there is no undo pattern for agent purchases.
buyer: Agent-card issuers and agent apps (as a feature), not end users
wedge: Personal agents that hold virtual cards
wow: The agent says 'buying 3 flights, cancel?' out loud, and one spoken word rolls it back on screen.

label: API mashup
take: Persona-driven LLM usability testing already exists as research systems, and this chains computer use, Figma and Listen Labs without adding a validated core.
reasoning: The agents do the work through Anthropic's computer-use API and the output is a Figma overlay; the team's glue is logging where an agent stalls. UXAgent and WebProber already run persona agents against live sites and report usability issues. Computer-use agents get stuck for their own reasons (slow screenshots, mis-clicks), so without calibration against real human sessions each 'death' may be an agent artifact, and a swarm of computer-use sessions is slow and costly inside 36 hours.
red_flag: Agent stuck-points are not validated against human ones, so a judge can dismiss every death as an agent bug.
components: Claude computer-use persona agents (API), task scripts per persona (prompt), stuck-point detection from action logs (glue, light original), Figma overlay (API), Listen Labs interviews at choke points (API)
hard_core: Aggregating agent failure points into a heatmap. Modest, and the key question (do agent failures predict human failures?) is unanswered.

label: Nice to have
take: Real problem, weak proxy: simulated humans are not humans, but AI shoppers are real customers you can actually test with.

Aiming the same swarm at the AI agents that now shop on these sites (pivot B-P7) measures a real, growing customer instead of a simulation.
red_flag: Findings from simulated users are hard to trust, so teams will still run real tests.

status_quo: Moderated tests, analytics funnels and session replay; research systems such as UXAgent already simulate thousands of LLM users, and UX researchers found the simulated behavior useful but not fully realistic.
solution: Claude computer-use personas try tasks; stuck points become deaths on a Figma overlay; AI interviews at the worst choke points.
optimizes: Conversion lost to UX friction (Baymard estimates large sites could gain about 35% conversion from better checkout design) and researcher hours.
who: Product and UX teams at web companies; a large segment.
harm: Teams may trust stereotyped synthetic 'grandma' personas over real users, baking model bias into design decisions.

reasoning: Synthetic Society (YC), Uxia and Talp already sell AI personas that click through products, and practitioners doubt LLMs mimic human behavior (Userbrain's 2026 experiment). Testing actual AI shopping agents makes the result true by construction and gives merchants a reason to pay.

prior_art: Synthetic Society (YC S25, AI agents as simulated users for QA and UX); Uxia (pre-seed Nov 2025, persona usability feedback); Talp (2026 pre-seed, AI personas on websites); Brox.ai (synthetic users navigating sites)
why_now: Computer-use models can now navigate real websites end to end.
buyer: PMs and UX researchers
model: SaaS per seat or per run
one_liner: Synthetic usability tests with a death map
wow: The 'grandma' agent dies three times on the same modal and the heatmap glows red there.

label: New angle
take: Unforgettable for two minutes and a weak company; per-minute voice cost and phone UX cap the market.

But consumer voice games are a hard business: reported Cartesia agent pricing of about $0.06 per minute plus telephony means every player-hour costs money, and audio-only retention is unproven. prior_art: The Parlor (AI Tinkerers hackathon, multiplayer voice-narrated mystery); Playworlds (voice-first single-player, Steam); GenFable (text MMO with AI narration)

take: A fresh, well-evidenced angle with textbook sponsor fit, but 'who pays?' has no answer as written; sell it to agent-card issuers (C-P3).
reasoning: SPLX (now part of Zscaler) and JFrog showed sites can serve AI agents a different page, and only tiny MCP tools check merchants today, so continuous paired measurement is open. A public trust index is a weak business: OpenAI or Perplexity can build it and consumers will not pay. The parties who lose money when an agent buys from a cheat are the new agent-card issuers, which gives a per-authorization model.
red_flag: No payer as written, and real-site cheating may be too rare to show in 36 hours.
prior_art: SPLX AI-targeted cloaking research (SPLX acquired by Zscaler, Nov 2025); JFrog / arXiv 'parallel-poisoned web' for AI agents; storefront-guard and Otr Protocol (small MCP merchant-trust tools); Princeton/UW study: shopping agents pick pricier sponsored options
why_now: Agentic checkout is live, AI-targeted cloaking is documented, and payment networks built buyer-side trust (Visa TAP) but not merchant-side.
buyer: Unclear as written; agent platforms may build it in-house
one_liner: Does this store show your agent the same page it shows you?
wow: A judge flips the cloak switch; 20 seconds later the trust score drops and the shopping agent refuses to buy.

label: Real system
take: A real system with a measurable core (breach rate versus service rate, with ground-truth settlement), though the game and the dataset sit close to Tensor Trust and Lakera's Agent Breaker.
reasoning: Coins move only when Claude's tool call reaches a validating reducer, so every attempt has a ground-truth outcome, and forcing guards to serve Claude-played customers turns the game into a security-versus-utility measurement that Tensor Trust's 'access granted' format lacks. That is an original loop someone has to engineer and balance, and reducers being unable to call out (only beta procedures can) confirms the worker design is necessary. The dataset alone is not new, so the value must be the utility constraint and Vault-Bench.
red_flag: Turnout and balance: with few real players the data is bot self-play, and the guard itself is a copyable prompt.
components: SpacetimeDB module with atomic transfer reducers, scheduled customer reducers and private tables (original game logic on sponsor tech), guard workers calling Claude with tools (API plus prompt), Claude-played legitimate customers (prompt), technique and break-turn labeler (prompt), Vault-Bench replay harness measuring breach vs service rate (original), mobile client and big screen (UI), Cartesia voices (API)
hard_core: An authoritative real-time economy where an LLM tool call is the only way money moves, under a service-rate constraint that stops guards from refusing everyone, feeding a breach-versus-service benchmark.

label: Nice to have
take: A great weekend game, but players will not come back after Sunday and the dataset adds modestly to existing ones.
reasoning: Entertainment and the data both have value, and the multi-turn, tool-using setup is better than single-shot games. But no company's agent gets safer from the public game, and the buyers for crowd jailbreak data already have Gandalf-scale corpora. Pivot B-P3 points the crowd at real customers' agents.
red_flag: Impact ends when the event does.
problem: Builders of agents that hold money lack realistic social-engineering attack data; players want a fun social game.
status_quo: Freysa (one guard, 482 attempts, about $47K lost), Gandalf, Tensor Trust and HackAPrompt, plus lab red-teaming.
solution: Multiplayer vaults guarded by player-configured Claude agents; every breach becomes labeled exploit data and a Vault-Bench replay.
optimizes: Fun, plus labeled authorization-exploit data with ground-truth outcomes.
who: Hackathon players for a weekend; a small number of eval researchers.
harm: A public exploit dataset is dual-use; risk of becoming a jailbreak farm.

label: Better execution
take: The best crowd demo in the pool on the most-done concept: Tensor Trust is already a multiplayer bank-vault game from Berkeley.
reasoning: The vault's prior-art line calls Tensor Trust single-player; it is not. Its players defend accounts with prompts and attack each other's for money, and the paper released 563K attacks. Gray Swan relaunched its arena with $300K for agent hacking two days before Cal Hacks, sponsored by Anthropic, so the data story is taken too. Keep it only as a SpacetimeDB and Supercell track play if those prizes are the richest.
red_flag: Berkeley judges know Tensor Trust is multiplayer; repeating the 'single-player' line will cost credibility.
prior_art: Tensor Trust (Berkeley; multiplayer game where players attack each other's LLM-guarded bank accounts; 563K attacks released); Gandalf: Agent Breaker (Lakera; tool-using agent levels); Freysa (talked out of about $47K, Nov 2024); Gray Swan Arena 2.0 ($300K agent-attack challenge launched Oct 20, 2026, sponsored by Anthropic, Meta and Google DeepMind); HackAPrompt 2.0
why_now: Agents with wallets are being socially engineered.
buyer: Players (game) or labs (data); both already served
one_liner: Tensor Trust with tools and a live economy
wow: Judges scan a QR code, talk Gary the teller out of coins, and watch coins fly across the big screen.

label: API mashup
take: AppointmentTrader already auctions reservations with predicted prices, and states are moving to fine unauthorized resale; this adds a phone voice.

red_flag: Prior art plus legal headwinds, and no core.
components: Cartesia voice agent on the host phone (API), queue-position pricing (glue or a simple auction), SpacetimeDB waitlist state (glue), Visa payment (API), Fetch agents (API)
hard_core: none as written; a queue-position auction could be one, but it is not specified.

label: Not needed

reasoning: The pain (waiting) is mild and the people who would pay are few. The only party with authority, the restaurant, has shown it does not want this, so impact is negative for most diners.
red_flag: Legal and restaurant opposition.
problem: Diners want to skip a long restaurant waitlist; others would sell their spot.
status_quo: Waitlist apps that text when a table is ready; reservation resale is banned in New York (Restaurant Reservation Anti-Piracy Act) and restaurants oppose it.

who: Diners at a few hot restaurants.

label: Better execution
take: Reservation resale exists and drew a New York ban; a restaurant-run version is legal but culturally risky.

wedge: High-demand walk-in restaurants with long waitlists
wow: A judge calls the host line and hears 'skip ahead for $12, or take $8 to give up your spot'.

label: Wrapper
take: Meta announced 'remember where you parked' memory for Ray-Ban Meta in 2024; this rebuilds the platform's own feature on hardware you may not have.

label: Nice to have
take: A universal but minor annoyance, solved only for people wearing camera glasses all day.
reasoning: The problem is frequent but costs minutes, and trackers already cover the high-value items. The fix requires continuous recording, a big privacy cost for a small gain.
red_flag: Hardware-gated and privacy-heavy for a small win.
problem: Someone loses their keys, phone or glasses several times a week.
status_quo: Bluetooth trackers for tagged items, retracing steps; one survey puts searching at about 16 minutes per item and roughly 17 hours a year.
solution: Glasses log where you set things down; ask out loud and on-device search answers in milliseconds.
optimizes: Minutes searching for misplaced items.
who: Everyone has the problem; only glasses owners get the fix.

label: Already exists
take: Meta's own glasses already do this; Meta's judges shipped it.
reasoning: Meta announced glasses memory for parking spots and visual reminders in 2024. Faster on-device search is an improvement only Meta can distribute.
red_flag: The sponsor's product already does it.
prior_art: Meta AI on Ray-Ban Meta glasses remembers where you parked and creates reminders from what you see (since 2024)
why_now: Meta already shipped it.
buyer: Consumers, already served by Meta
one_liner: Find My for your stuff, via glasses
wow: Ask 'where are my keys?' and get an answer in milliseconds.

label: Thin glue
take: Attack-path analysis is a graph problem BloodHound has solved for years; an LLM red-teamer on a synthetic map with a Clash skin adds no core.
reasoning: Finding which wall the attacker walked around is path search over a graph with edge preconditions, which BloodHound already does on real Active Directory data. An LLM raiding the map is slower and less complete than a search. The stronger version would compute the optimal wall placement (a min-cut) and grade players against it, but that is a training toy, and 'your real network map' will not be real at a hackathon.
red_flag: The AI does what a graph algorithm does better, on a synthetic network.
components: Network map import (glue), wall placement UI (game), AI red-team raid (LLM agent over the graph, or path search), replay showing the bypassed wall (UI), SpacetimeDB state (API)
hard_core: Attack-path search over a segmented network graph. Real logic, but a graph search does it better than an LLM agent.

label: Nice to have
take: A fun wrapper on breach-and-attack simulation, a category that already exists without the game.
reasoning: Lateral movement is a real risk, but the security value here is the simulated raid, which existing tools provide. The game skin helps training engagement, a modest gain.
red_flag: Security teams will not put their real network map in a game.
problem: A security team cannot easily see whether its segmentation rules would stop an attacker moving laterally.
status_quo: Breach-and-attack simulation tools, penetration tests, and segmentation vendors' own maps.
solution: A Clash-style game where your base is your real network map; place segmentation walls, an AI red-team agent raids, and the replay shows which wall it walked around.
optimizes: Understanding of segmentation gaps; training engagement.
who: Security teams at mid-size and large enterprises.
harm: Uploading a real network map into a game is itself a sensitive exposure; an AI raid planner is dual-use.

label: New angle
take: A memorable way to show segmentation working, but it is a visualization layer on breach simulation, and the natural buyer is Illumio.
reasoning: Cyber ranges and gamified red/blue platforms exist, but I found no one framing segmentation as Clash-style base defense, so the demo will stand out with Illumio, Armadin and Supercell. As a company it would compete with cyber-range vendors like SimSpace and with Illumio's own tools, with monthly use at best.
red_flag: A real network map is data nobody will hand a hackathon team; with a fake map it is just a game.
prior_art: DefAtt (gamified red/blue team platform); SimSpace (cyber range red teaming); MIT Lincoln Lab: co-evolution of attack and segmentation defense; 2026 arXiv study of AI attackers against segmented networks
why_now: AI red-team agents can now raid networks on their own; one 2026 study found segmentation stretched an AI attacker's time to compromise from about 4 to about 48 hours.
buyer: Security teams planning segmentation; segmentation vendors for training and visualization
wedge: Teams in the middle of a microsegmentation rollout
one_liner: Clash of Clans for network segmentation
wow: The AI raider walks around the wall you placed and the replay shows the exact lateral path.

label: Real system
take: It removes the tautology in the original: enforcement does not depend on wording, so 'what if they reword it?' is answered by design, and the utility column proves you did not just delete the tool. Each part does what it is good at: the LLM searches for attacks (a script cannot), and the engine enforces (an LLM should not). It is CaMeL's information-flow idea turned into a product for finance agents, with a measured result instead of a demo-only PASS.
components: Victim AP agent on Claude Agent SDK (API), tree-search attacker over tactic x channel (original loop plus prompt), Cartesia Line voice channel (API), provenance-tagging tool proxy and policy engine (original), Claude policy proposer (prompt), held-out variant generator plus breach/utility harness (original), Visa sandbox payment (API), scorecard (glue/UI)
hard_core: Deterministic provenance enforcement on money-moving tool arguments, plus a statistical breach-versus-utility evaluation over generated held-out attacks.

label: Emerging
take: A fix that holds no matter how the attack is worded, aimed at the most expensive fraud in finance, but it still protects tomorrow's agent AP desks rather than the human desks where the roughly $3B a year is lost today.

label: New angle
take: The most defensible version of Fire Drill: CaMeL and FIDES-style information-flow control exist only as research, with no product found, so a provenance policy for money-moving agents is open ground. The breach-versus-utility table wins technical judges, but the fix is less visible on stage than a phone ringing; it works best as the trigger for C-P1's callback.

label: Real system
take: The hard core is now original engineering that is not one API call, and it is measurable: precision and recall per hiding technique on a labeled corpus. The live moment is not staged, because a judge can paste any hiding trick into a page and watch it stripped before the agent reads it. Say the limit out loud: it stops hidden instructions, not visible ones.
components: Bright Data Scraping Browser or Playwright rendering (API), perceptual-visibility engine over computed style, layout and pixel sampling (original), DOM-text versus perceivable-text delta (original), Claude borderline classifier (prompt), MCP fetch server (glue), Elastic findings index (API), paired-identity crawl study (original, background)
hard_core: Computing the human-perceivable text layer of a rendered page and diffing it against what the agent would otherwise ingest.

label: Emerging
take: The same defensive turn I proposed for Two-Face, made concrete with a measurable visibility engine; it blocks a documented injection class on every page, and it is honest that visible manipulation still gets through.

label: Better execution
take: A good live moment (paste any hiding trick and watch it vanish), but render-based hidden-text stripping already exists: a Chrome extension does it and Claude Code users have requested it. Browser-agent vendors will build it in, so it is a feature, not a company.

label: Real system
take: The AI does the hard reasoning (finding an input that exposes a subtle behavior change) and a script does the judging, which is exactly the split the Anthropic judge looks for. The verdict is mechanically verifiable, the catch rate on seeded mutants is a number, and it targets a real, growing workload: the flood of agent-written refactor PRs.
components: Claude/Factory Droid hunter agents writing differential tests (API plus prompt), sandboxed base-versus-head test runner with flake filter (original), mutation-injection benchmark for catch rate (original), GitHub check gate and report (glue), Greptile context for hunters (API), optional x402 bounty (API)
hard_core: A differential-testing oracle (passes on base, fails on head, stable across reruns) that turns an LLM's bug hunt into machine-verified proof, measured by catch rate on seeded regressions.

label: Urgent
take: A real, daily workload (agent refactors and dependency bumps) with a reliable test that proves regressions, but it covers a narrower slice of bugs than review in general.

label: New angle
take: A sound oracle aimed at a growing workload, but Testora (ICSE 2026) and DiffTestGen already generate tests that expose behavior changes between base and PR, so this turns research into a CI check that code-review vendors can copy.

label: Emerging
take: Prompt injection cannot be fully prevented (OpenAI, NCSC), so detection and containment is where damage gets cut; a legitimate agent has no reason to call 'export_all_customers_decoy', so a touch is a near-zero-false-positive signal, the same reason honeytokens work in classic security.
problem: A company's support or coding agent is prompt-injected by a ticket or web page and starts using its real tools to pull and leak data, as in the GitHub MCP and Supabase MCP demonstrations.
status_quo: Injection filters that miss novel attacks, least-privilege configs, and human confirmations users click through.
solution: Canary tools and data seeded into each agent's toolset; any touch triggers instant tool-access quarantine plus a trace back to the poisoned input.
optimizes: Time to detect a hijacked agent and records exfiltrated per injection; alert false-positive rate.
who: Every company running agents with MCP tools on private data; tens of thousands and growing.
harm: Decoy data must be obviously synthetic so it never resembles real PII; aggressive quarantine can halt business workflows.

label: Thin glue
take: Honeytokens inside your own fleet are a sound signal, but the decoy tool and alert-on-call already ship (Thinkst's MCP Canarytoken, Beelzebub), and an attacker after one payment redirect never touches 'export_all_customers_decoy', so coverage is thin and the demo attack is one you aim at the decoy.

label: Already exists
take: Agent Canary already plants decoy MCP tools and canary files that a hijacked agent will touch, and HoneyMCP and Beelzebub do the same; adding quarantine is a small step on an existing open-source idea.

label: Emerging
take: It blocks a documented attack class (indirect injection through web content, which OpenAI says will never be fully solved) instead of measuring a price-discrimination problem no one has shown is common, so it has impact even if no cheating store is found.
problem: An agent shopping or researching for a person reads text the person never sees and gets steered, overcharged or hijacked.
status_quo: Agents ingest raw page content and rely on model-level injection resistance.
solution: A human-render parity filter in front of the model, a log of what was stripped and why, and a merchant risk score exposed over MCP.
optimizes: Successful manipulations or injections per 1,000 pages an agent browses; overpayment on agent purchases.
who: Agent builders and agent-commerce platforms; every shopping or browsing agent.
harm: Stripping 'hidden' text can also remove screen-reader text and break accessibility content; a shared risk index can wrongly tar merchants.

label: Real system
take: Same defensive core as my A-P2: a human-perceivable render layer computed per page is original engineering that works on any page, is measurable per hiding technique, and needs no staged cheater.

label: Better execution
take: A slightly better business than A-P2, because the shared merchant risk index becomes a data asset, but the shield itself is a feature that render-based extensions and agent vendors already cover, and a defensive filter has no clear payer.

label: Emerging
take: Turns a one-weekend game into a recurring service for a buyer with real exposure (agents holding money get socially engineered; Freysa lost about $47K), and gives players a reason to return: payouts.
problem: A team shipping an agent that can move money does not know how it holds up against creative human manipulation.
status_quo: Internal red-teaming, automated scanners and occasional crowd competitions.
solution: A bounty arena with ground-truth tool-call outcomes and auto-generated regression tests per customer agent.
optimizes: Breach rate before launch; cost per discovered exploit.
who: Startups and enterprises deploying agents with wallets or payment tools; hundreds to low thousands today.
harm: Exploits found against one customer may work on others; bounty findings must stay private until fixed.

label: Thin glue
take: It drops Vault Heist's real core (the service-rate constraint) for a bounty marketplace that Gray Swan already runs at scale for agents, and at a hackathon the 'company agent' will be your own.

label: Already exists
take: This is HackerOne's AI red-teaming and AI bug-bounty business (H1 Agentic Pentest launched Jan 2026) and Gray Swan's private arenas; there is a real buyer, but incumbents already serve it.

label: Urgent
take: Targets the costliest pains for circle members, credit invisibility and default risk, with a model already shown to work (Mission Asset Fund: 68,000+ participants, average +168 credit-score points).
problem: An immigrant family saving through a tanda builds no credit history and risks a member skipping out after taking the pot.
status_quo: Informal circles on trust; a few nonprofits formalize and report them.
solution: Agent-administered circles with KYC, reminders, a default-cover pool and credit-bureau furnishing.
optimizes: Credit-score gain per member and default rate per circle.
who: Savings-group users worldwide and US immigrants without credit files; millions.
harm: Reporting missed payments can hurt members' credit; KYC can exclude undocumented members who rely on circles most.

label: API mashup
take: A tanda ledger plus CRS data furnishing plus reminder agents: Mission Asset Fund already runs the model, and nothing here needs an LLM or original engineering.

label: Already exists
take: Mission Asset Fund's Lending Circles already run zero-interest circles and report payments to all three bureaus, for free, so a venture-backed copy faces a nonprofit that costs users nothing.

label: Emerging
take: Agent cards are shipping now (Ramp on Visa Intelligent Commerce, Mastercard Agent Pay) and agents do buy things unasked (Operator's $31 eggs), so behavioral controls and attribution are an emerging, recurring finance need.
problem: A finance lead gives 20 agents virtual cards and discovers only at month-end that one looped and re-bought the same API credits all week.
status_quo: Static card caps and merchant locks; manual reconciliation of agent charges.
solution: Behavioral rules and anomaly detection on agent spend, an instant freeze, and automatic attribution of each charge to its task or commit.
optimizes: Unauthorized or runaway agent spend; hours spent reconciling agent charges.
who: Companies issuing cards or wallets to agents; early but growing.
harm: False freezes stall legitimate work; detailed spend graphs expose employee activity.

label: Thin glue
take: Per-task budgets and freezes are card-issuer features Ramp already sells, loop and duplicate checks are rules, and charge-to-task attribution is a tag at authorization time, so the AI is optional.

label: Better execution
take: A real buyer exists today, but card issuers (Mercury Agent Cards, Ramp, Agentcard, Allowance) already ship limits and freezes, so loop detection and per-task attribution are features they will bundle.

label: Urgent
take: AI review is ignored because it is noisy (more developers distrust AI accuracy than trust it); proof-backed findings raise precision, cutting reviewer time while catching real bugs in agent code (Veracode: flaws in 45% of tasks), with no collusion incentive.
problem: A maintainer reviewing an agent-written PR gets ten speculative AI comments and ignores them all, including the one real bug.
status_quo: Low-precision AI reviewers and overloaded human review.
solution: The reviewer must produce a reproducing test; only proven issues are posted, with the test attached.
optimizes: Precision of review comments, escaped defects, reviewer minutes per PR.
who: Teams merging AI-written PRs; millions of developers.
harm: Bugs that are hard to test (race conditions, authorization logic) go unreported, creating false confidence.

label: Real system
take: Sandboxed test generation and execution as the gate for every comment is real, but outside regressions a failing test only proves the reviewer's assertion, which may be wrong, so the oracle is weaker than it sounds.

label: Better execution
take: Requiring proof before a review comment is already practiced (Claude Code Review's verification step, 'no proof, no report' review skills, CodeAnt's reproduction steps); without the pay-per-proven-bug pricing in C-P4 nothing sets it apart in a crowded category.

label: Emerging
take: AI-referred shopping is growing fast (AI referrals to US retail up 693% year over year in the 2025 holidays) and agents struggle with cluttered choices; merchants can count lost agent orders directly, and fixes such as labeled buttons and structured data often help screen-reader users too.
problem: A merchant's site works for people, but agents stall on pop-ups, unlabeled buttons or CAPTCHAs, so agent-driven orders silently fail.
status_quo: Merchants test for humans only; analytics cannot see failed agent sessions.
solution: An agent swarm, a failure heatmap, a ranked fix list and a re-test.
optimizes: Agent checkout completion rate and revenue from the agent channel.
who: E-commerce merchants; a large segment with an early but growing need.
harm: Optimizing for agents can tempt merchants to remove bot protection, helping scalpers and fraud bots.

label: Thin glue
take: Fixes Death Heatmap's validity problem (agent failures are now the real failures), but it is still computer-use runs plus logging, and lab agents like Claude computer use are proxies for production shopping agents, not the same thing.

label: New angle
take: This is the same pivot as my C-P2, reached independently: merchants are a real payer with weekly use, and Shopify's free readiness checker is static, not a live agent run, but agent traffic is still small enough that budgets are early.

label: Urgent
take: Covers where the roughly $3B a year of reported BEC losses happen today (human AP desks that skip callbacks or dial the number in the fraudulent email) as well as tomorrow's agent AP, and the metric is concrete: redirected payments blocked. It follows the rule AP vendors already state, that bank changes must be verified out of band and never by the agent that received the request.
problem: An AP clerk or AP agent receives a convincing 'we changed banks' email or an urgent CFO call and pays the fraudster.
status_quo: Callback policies skipped under deadline pressure, verification networks such as Eftsure and Trustpair, and awareness training.
solution: Drills plus an automatic, independent voice callback to the verified contact on file, a payment freeze until confirmation, and a re-drill to prove the control holds.
optimizes: Redirected-payment losses (about $123K per reported BEC complaint in 2025) and the share of bank changes verified out of band.
who: AP teams at mid-market and enterprise companies; 63% of organizations reported BEC targeting in AFP's survey.
harm: Synthetic CFO voices and attack scripts are dual-use; callbacks must never use contact details supplied in the request itself.

label: Thin glue
take: A callback on the number of record is the right control, but it is a registry lookup, a Cartesia call and a payment hold, and drilling human AP desks is existing KnowBe4/Abnormal territory, so it adds a product but no core.

label: New angle
take: This converges with my C-P1, which is a strong signal. Covering human AP desks widens today's market (IC3 counted about $3B of BEC losses in 2025), but it also walks into KnowBe4, Trustpair and Eftsure territory, so pitch it as agent-native and treat the human desk as an expansion.

label: New angle
take: It turns a periodic drill into per-transaction infrastructure with daily, usage-priced demand, and gives a land-and-expand motion: the drill shows the hole, Callback closes it on every payment. The demo gains a second phone moment: the judge as a fake CFO makes the agent cave; after the patch, a teammate's 'vendor' phone rings at the table, denies the change, and the payment is blocked on screen. Trustpair and Eftsure verify bank details for human AP teams, so the agent-native API is the new angle; they are also the competitors to name.
prior_art: Coval ($28M Series A), Hamming, Cekura (voice agent testing); Gray Swan ($40M Series A, automated agent red-teaming); KnowBe4 Agent Risk Manager; AIUC ($40M Series A, AIUC-1 certification with quarterly testing); Trustpair and Eftsure (vendor bank-account verification for human AP teams); Spendflo bank-detail change verification agent
why_now: AP agents now change vendor records and approve payments, BEC losses were $2.77B in 2024, and Cartesia Line makes programmatic outbound verification calls cheap.
buyer: AP-automation vendors and mid-market finance teams running AP agents; insurers and auditors (AIUC-1-style) as a channel
model: Per-agent SaaS for drills plus a per-verification usage fee for Callback
wedge: Vendor bank-detail changes handled by AP agents, the highest-loss business email compromise action
one_liner: A pen test and a callback desk for AI finance agents
wow: The judge talks the AP agent into a payout redirect; after the patch, a teammate's phone rings as the 'vendor', denies the change, and the payment is blocked live.

label: Thin glue
take: Slightly deeper than B-P8 because the rail refuses to release funds without a signed attestation, a deterministic gate, but Trustpair and Eftsure already verify bank details and there is no breach-versus-utility measurement.

label: Urgent
take: The same move as my B-P8: a callback on every payment, using the contact already on file, attacks the biggest documented payments fraud today, and it should be sold to human AP desks as well as agents.

label: New angle
take: The result is true by construction (these are the real agents that will shop), merchants already pay to be visible to AI (Profound raised $58.5M on that thesis), Shopify's free readiness checker is static rather than a live agent run, and weekly re-runs after each deploy give recurring use. It shares Two-Face's crawl engine, so the two could later become one two-sided product.
prior_art: Shopify agent readiness tool (free, static checks); EPAM agentic commerce activation assessment (consulting); Profound ($35M Series B, AI search visibility); Synthetic Society (YC S25)
why_now: Agentic checkout protocols are live, and Forter reported agentic activity up about 2,100% in six months.
buyer: DTC e-commerce brands and their agencies
model: SaaS per store, tiered by number of agent runs
wedge: Shopify Plus DTC brands already worried about agent traffic
wow: Six agents race to check out on a demo store, four die at the same popup, one fix ships, and on the re-run they all buy.

label: Thin glue
take: Same engine as B-P7 with a better buyer; the real work would be making stochastic agent runs reproducible enough to attribute revenue loss, and the pivot does not say how.

label: Emerging
take: Matches my B-P7: it measures a real and fast-growing customer, AI shoppers, with a revenue number, but agent-driven sales are still a small base.

label: New angle
take: It names a payer and a per-transaction usage pattern. Visa TAP and Forter help merchants trust agents; nobody sells the reverse to issuers. It keeps the cloak-switch moment and the textbook Bright Data and Elastic fit.
prior_art: SPLX AI-targeted cloaking research (acquired by Zscaler); JFrog 'parallel-poisoned web' research; storefront-guard and Otr Protocol MCP merchant-trust tools; Forter (merchant-side agent traffic detection); Visa Trusted Agent Protocol (merchants verifying agents)

take: It names a buyer (teams drowning in AI-review false positives), daily usage, and a distinct price point in a crowded category; I found no reviewer that bills only for bugs proven by a failing test.
prior_art: Claude Code Review (multi-agent PR review with a verification step); Greptile ($1 per review after 50, per 2026 pricing roundups); Staking-backed bug bounties on Immunefi
why_now: AI review costs collapsed and noisy AI findings flood reviewers; x402 makes per-proof micro-payouts trivial.
buyer: Engineering managers at startups using coding agents
model: Per-proven-bug fee with a monthly cap
wedge: Teams already using Factory Droids or Claude Code who ignore most AI review comments
wow: A judge opens a PR with a planted bug; three reviewer agents stake, one posts a failing test in about a minute, CI goes red and a USDC payout appears on the Base Sepolia explorer.

label: Thin glue
take: Same proof-by-failing-test core as B-P6, but tying payment to 'first valid proof' makes the unsound oracle carry money, and the staking and reviewer-marketplace layers add integration surface, not depth.

take: Proof-backed review answers a real noise problem, but the pricing and staking layer adds nothing to impact and brings back some gaming risk compared with a plain proof-only reviewer.
